NAMING GOD, PAST AND PRESENT

WHAT THIS CHAPTER COVERS
- Three traditional and three contemporary images of God.
- Religious interpretations of human experience: prophetic, mystical, holy, poetic and aesthetic - with examples.
- Traditional proofs of God: St Anselm, St Thomas Aquinas, St Bonaventure, Avicenna and Isaac Newton (Higher Level).

KEY TERMS
- Images of God: physical or mental representations of God.
- Omnipotent: all-powerful.
- Prophet: a man or woman who tries to communicate who God is and what God asks of people, especially justice and peace.
- Marginalised: people on the margins or edges of society because of poverty and/or inequality.
- Mystical interpretation: seeking God by going on a journey inwards.
- Holy: another word for sacred.
- Poetic and aesthetic: an artistic understanding of life. Poets interpret life through poetry; aesthetic relates to the arts (music, painting, sculpture). Some artists believe God can be expressed through these.
- Ontological argument: our existence means a more perfect being must exist; if God existed only in the mind and not in reality, he would not be the greatest being conceivable.
- Proofs for the existence of God: philosophical arguments suggesting it is reasonable to believe in God. The most famous are those of St Thomas Aquinas.
- Quote: T.S. Eliot - 'We shall not cease from exploration, and the end of all of our exploring will be to arrive, where we started and know the place for the first time.'

INTRODUCTION
- Chapter 7: divine revelation is God communicating with humanity to reveal who God is and his plan for creation; in it people find the meaning and purpose of life.
- Putting the experience of God into words is an ongoing challenge.
- Humans use symbol and metaphor to describe what is beyond understanding - e.g. God as father, mother or powerful leader, depending on context; also art, poetry, music and dance.
- The 'footprints of the divine' (Chapter 7): beauty, truth, love and goodness.
- Some scholars say many adults keep childlike images of God that never change - this can be problematic.

TRADITIONAL IMAGES OF GOD (JUDEO-CHRISTIAN)
- Islam is the exception: God is never portrayed in any image; he is the absolute one, nothing compares to him. He is known through immaterial attributes like 'holy' or 'merciful' - his 'Ninety-nine beautiful names'.
1. GOD AS FATHER
- Jesus called God his father, using the intimate word 'Abba'.
- Luke 11:1-4 - the prayer Jesus taught: 'Father, hallowed be your name.'
- Shows God caring for humanity as a parent cares for a child - protecting and guiding. A familiar image, but only one part of God's identity, which can never be fully known in this life.
- Art: God the Father (Luca Cambiaso); God the Father and God the Son (Pieter de Grebber); First Day of Creation (Julius Schnorr von Carolsfeld). Images like these are used in prayer and worship; there are also contemporary versions.
2. CREATOR GOD
- From the Old Testament: in Genesis God creates the world and humanity and sees that it is good.
- 'So God created humankind in his image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them.' (Gn 1:27)
- Links God to the beauty and diversity of nature; expresses the belief that God existed before creation.
- Art: The Creation of Adam by Michelangelo (Sistine Chapel); God Creating the Sun and Moon (after Michelangelo); contemporary: The Hand of God by Bruce Rolff.
3. GOD AS ALL-POWERFUL PROTECTOR
- From the Old Testament; omnipotent = all-powerful.
- Arose in a time of great difficulty for the Jewish people - they needed a powerful God to save them from slavery and oppression. Expresses that God looks after his people.
- An example of historical context shaping images of God.
THE 'MALENESS' OF TRADITIONAL IMAGES
- Christians believe God transcends the difference between the sexes: 'God is neither man nor woman' (Catechism of the Catholic Church).
- Male images show the limits of human language and the patriarchal societies where they began.
- Over-emphasising one image can cause problems; it is important to understand the image as Jesus presented and lived it.

CONTEMPORARY IMAGES OF GOD
- Many are not really 'new' but rediscovered or rejuvenated.
1. GOD AS MOTHER
- Isaiah 42:14 - God like a woman in labour.
- Isaiah 49:14-15 - God like a woman who cannot forget the child she has borne.
- Luke 13:20-21 - God like a woman baking bread.
- Deut 32:11-12 - a mother eagle; Deut 32:18 - God gives birth; Is 66:13 - a comforting mother; Ps 131:2 - mother to a weaned child; Hos 11:3-4 - a mother teaching her child to walk.
- Matthew 23:37 and Luke 13:34 - a mother hen: 'How often have I desired to gather your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!'
- Art: Trinity - After Rublev, Southwark by Meg Wroe.
2. GOD AS LIBERATOR
- From the Old Testament - the call of Moses (Exodus 3:7-10).
- Empowering for people who experience oppression. Jesus' prophetic message of peace and justice spoke to people enslaved by cruel systems.
- God takes pity on the suffering and supports their struggle for a just world.
- 'Go Down, Moses' - a Spiritual created by Black Americans during and after slavery: 'When Israel was in Egypt's land, Let my people go ... Tell ole Pharaoh Let my people go.'
3. GOD AS LOVE
- The parable of the prodigal son (Luke 15:11-32) shows God as unconditional love.
- The human desire for loving relationships makes this image powerful. Love is abstract and open to interpretation, so it is accessible to believers today.
- For Christians, God's unconditional love is bound up with Jesus' life, death and resurrection.
- Art: The Return of the Prodigal Son (Rembrandt); The Cross (Alex Tsuper).
SUMMARY OF IMAGES
- Traditional images speak of God's power and fatherly love (father, creator, all-powerful protector).
- Contemporary images speak of God's love and motherly care (mother, love); some are political (liberator).
POEM: 'A PRAYER TO THE GOD WHO FELL FROM HEAVEN' - JOHN SHEA
- First image: a distant God 'tight-fisted in the sky' watching us 'with all the patience of a pipe smoker' - prayer would be 'like a golden bullet aimed at your heart'.
- 'But the story says you cried and so heavy was the tear you fell with it to earth' - God came among us (the Incarnation).
- Then images of a close God: 'like a baritone in a bar', 'twisting every straight line into Picasso', 'stealing kisses from pinched lips, holding our hand in the dark'.
- Prayer becomes relaxed: God with 'large, open hands spreading my life before me like a Sunday tablecloth' and 'pulling up a chair'. 'The secret is out. You are home.'

RELIGIOUS INTERPRETATIONS OF HUMAN EXPERIENCE
- Prophetic, mystical, holy, poetic and aesthetic. They are ways of engaging with the experience of the divine; they are interconnected and all are helpful in the search for meaning.

THE PROPHETIC INTERPRETATION
- Every generation produces prophets in response to injustice.
- A prophet examines and critiques society in the light of religious belief. They get energy and strength from prayer and reflection, call people to faith and conversion of heart, and seek to know God's will and share it for the good of all.
- Deeply political (seek structural change) but always rooted in prayer.
- Challenges the status quo (the way things are) and cries out for change - in behaviour, attitudes and lifestyle - for greater justice. Injustice that causes suffering offends God.
- Roots: Old Testament prophets Amos, Jeremiah and Isaiah; New Testament - John the Baptist and Jesus.
- Prophets are often 'voices in the wilderness' - ignored, criticised or marginalised, because people resist change that affects their wealth and status.
EXAMPLE: FR PETER MCVERRY SJ
- Jesuit priest who has worked with homeless people for many years; called one of the most prophetic voices in Ireland.
- In 1974, newly ordained, he chose to live and work in Dublin's inner city with a small group of Jesuits, working with young people from severely disadvantaged backgrounds - early school leavers, drug and alcohol abuse, crime, little hope.
- What he saw shocked him and challenged his own attitudes; it opened his eyes to a divided society.
- He questions a society that tolerates division and inequality; in the media he calls for a truly Christian response to poverty. Justice, and so peace, will come only when followers of Jesus live the challenging, radical Gospel values.
- Writes for national newspapers and religious publications.
- Set up the Peter McVerry Trust - a national housing and homeless charity to reduce homelessness and harm from substance misuse and social disadvantage; vision of an Ireland supporting all on the margins and their right to full inclusion.
- The Trust organised Ireland's first Empty Homes Conference (2017), hired Ireland's first full-time Vacant Homes Officer, has had more Empty Homes projects than any other Approved Housing Body; as of 2021 it delivers 61% of services under the 'Housing First' National Implementation Plan.
- 2013 talk at the International Eucharistic Congress: 'In a community that loves one another, there should be no one poor (unless all are poor); there should be no one homeless, no one lonely ... no one rejected or marginalised.'
- Book: The Meaning is in the Shadows - about Donal, Frank and John. Frank, homeless and in Health Board care, was refused the emergency service on his eighteenth birthday because he was now an adult, and spent the night in a doorway - 'Adulthood in the shadows.'
- People and politicians were too busy making and spending money to notice them. Those in the shadows are 'God's favourites'; Jesus too lived in the shadows - 'God became one of them.' We search for meaning everywhere but 'the meaning is in the shadows.'
- All Christians are called to be prophetic: in Baptism every Christian is anointed as priest, prophet and king, so all must speak out against injustice.
EXAMPLE: POPE FRANCIS
- Became pope in March 2013; a famous prophetic voice. He has turned Twitter into a prophetic medium (e.g. a 'tweetstorm' on social justice in October 2021). Involved in the refugee crisis, climate crisis and rights of women. 'The Church has come a long way from Jesus preaching on a hillside to a pope broadcasting through cyberspace.'

THE MYSTICAL INTERPRETATION
- Does not start with challenging society; it is an inner journey, leaving behind the world's distractions.
- Found in all faiths. The person seeks to know God personally and intensely. Uses imagination rather than logic; through meditation, prayer and contemplation one may experience God.
- Very popular today - perhaps due to the fast pace of life and growing materialism; people realise wealth and beauty don't guarantee happiness.
- Henri Nouwen: a modern example combining the mystical and the prophetic. Profound mystics always speak of care for others, compassion and love.
- Buddhism: a mystical interpretation of life, emphasising meditation. Life is always changing; happiness is not in wealth, possessions, beauty or fame. Freeing ourselves from these leads to enlightenment - Nirvana. Buddha: 'Peace comes from within. Do not seek it without.'
- Christians use meditation and contemplative prayer to experience God personally; this sustains daily life.
CHRISTIAN WOMEN MYSTICS
- St Catherine of Siena: one of the two patron saints of Italy; born 1347, second-youngest surviving child of twenty-five; joined the Dominican Order in 1363; died at thirty-three. Saying: 'Be who God meant you to be and you will set the world on fire.' Canonised 1461; Doctor of the Church 1970.
- St Therese of Lisieux: born in France, 1873; mystical union with Christ while preparing for First Holy Communion; entered the Carmelite Monastery of Lisieux in 1888; died at twenty-four; famous through her writings; 'The Little Flower'. Saying: 'What matters in life is not great deeds, but great love.' Canonised May 1925; Doctor of the Church (Pope John Paul II) 1997.
- These women grew close to God through prayer, fasting and contemplation; lived courageous, radical lives.
ISLAMIC MYSTICS (SUFI)
- Attar of Nishapur (thirteenth century): a man weeps to win God's pity; told God has no physical heart, he replies God 'is the owner of all the hearts which exist. Through the heart you can make your connection with God.'
- Rumi: 'I am not hidden in what is high or low ... I am hidden in the heart of the faithful. If you seek me, seek in these hearts.'
- Hafiz: 'I am happy even before I have a reason ... We have been in love with God for so very, very long.'

THE HOLY INTERPRETATION
- To see events in life as sacred - birth, death, marriage and life choices are events where God is present. Special times are celebrated through ritual and prayer; joys and sorrows are holy. Today's rituals have roots in the past.
- Christianity: the Sacraments - 'visible signs of invisible grace' - occasions when God's action is especially recognised and celebrated.
- Baptism: welcomes a new member; water of new life; white robes = new life in Christ.
- Funeral rite: death as the beginning of new life in Christ; comforts the grieving and expresses hope in the resurrection.
- Marriage: falling in love and committing to another is holy; the Church celebrates the sacred covenant of marriage in God's presence.
- Judaism: no Sacraments, but scriptures and rabbinic laws guide rites of passage, holy days and religious life.
- Brit milah: circumcision of a boy eight days after birth.
- Bar mitzvah (boys at thirteen) and bat mitzvah (girls at twelve) - coming of age.
- Badeken: the groom veils the bride before the wedding.
- Recitation of the Shema twice daily by Jewish men. Only Orthodox Jews observe all of these; brit milah and coming-of-age are common to all branches.
- Shabbat (Sabbath): the holiest day - rest from all work, a day of study and prayer, sundown Friday to sundown Saturday. No business or housework; food prepared beforehand; lights left on so no switch is touched.
- These moments are communal - God is present in a special way when his people gather.

THE POETIC AND AESTHETIC INTERPRETATION
- Artistic and creative people express their religious interpretation of life through poetry, music and art. Great beauty suggests God's presence. Art has expressed belief in God from earliest times.
- John Shea, 'A Prayer to the God Who Will Not Go Away' (from The Hour of the Unexpected): 'Lord, you are the poetry of wordless lives, the salting of tasteless purposes ... You are the tightening hope that someone has stretched a net beneath this high wire act of ours.' Theme: God gives purpose and meaning to life and protects and cares for us.
- Art from one faith can inspire others because its themes are universal.
- White Crucifixion by Marc Chagall - a favourite of Pope Francis. Chagall (born Moishe Segal in Vitebsk, now Belarus) was probably the most prominent Jewish painter of the twentieth century. It hangs in the Art Institute of Chicago. Jesus the Jew is crucified, wearing a tallit (prayer shawl), between communist soldiers storming a village (left) and Nazis desecrating a synagogue (right) - a victim of hatred from both sides.
- David Lyle Jeffrey ('The Christ of Marc Chagall'): for Chagall, Jesus on the cross represented the suffering of all Jewish people 'in an apparently God-forsaken world'. Pope Francis may love it because it makes us think of those martyred today - showing him as a prophetic voice.
- Lauren Ashley Daigle: American contemporary Christian singer-songwriter; combines a modern aesthetic with Christian themes. Her song 'You Say' (over 243 million YouTube views) is about identity - who we are in God's eyes even when the world says otherwise.

PROOFS OF GOD (HIGHER LEVEL)
- All the world religions have a rich intellectual tradition using science, mathematics, reason and logic.
- 'Proof' here is not verifiable scientific evidence and not blind faith - proofs are signposts in our thinking about God's existence.
ST ANSELM (1033-1109)
- Scholastic philosopher and theologian, born in Aosta, Italy; Archbishop of Canterbury 1093-1109; one of the first medieval scholars to try to prove God exists; 'father of scholasticism'.
- Started from belief in God; held that our existence means a more perfect being must exist; God is greater than anything we can conceive.
- Argument: (1) 'God' means the greatest conceivable being; (2) existing in reality is greater than existing only in the understanding; (3) therefore God must exist in reality.
- Since Immanuel Kant (1724-1804) this has been called the ontological argument. It may seem implausible today but has a definite logic.
ST THOMAS AQUINAS (1225-1274)
- Lived when reason was admired; wanted to make faith a reasonable subject of discussion. Five proofs:
- 1. Prime mover: nothing moves itself; there must be a first mover - God.
- 2. Cause of existence: nothing creates itself; there must be an uncreated creator - God, the first cause.
- 3. Necessary being: a being on which all others depend - God.
- 4. Degrees of perfection: for qualities like beauty or goodness there must be a perfect standard - God.
- 5. Supreme intelligence: the universe is ordered towards regular ends, so it must be directed by an intellect - God.
ST BONAVENTURE
- A Franciscan and contemporary of Aquinas. In The Journey of the Mind to God he combined reason and logic with religious experience; emphasised spiritual experience.
- Looked to the life of St Francis: Francis achieved an excellence that seemed beyond human, which suggests we can 'see and understand that the "best" is ... that than which nothing better can be imagined' (using Anselm's proof). If we can imagine the best, it must exist in the perfection of God.
- An inner journey: the believer is 'transported in ecstasy above the intellect' to a vision of God. Like Anselm's, not meant to convince unbelievers; religious experience is a necessary part.
AVICENNA (980-1037 CE)
- Medieval Muslim philosopher-scientist; one of the most influential in the medieval Islamic world.
- Proof of the Truthful: based on 'determinate things' - everything we experience depends on something else. Example: we exist but might not have; our parents brought us into existence. The whole physical universe is also dependent, so it needs an external cause - God. Very similar to Aquinas' 'uncreated creator'.
ISAAC NEWTON (1642-1727)
- English physicist of the Enlightenment; a scientist first, but saw God as an essential part of the system and believed he could prove God's existence.
- Asked: why has gravity not pulled all the planets into one mass? Because they were carefully placed - pointing to an intelligent, powerful being governing their movement so life is possible; a perfect intelligence.
- The Principles of Natural Philosophy (1687): 'This most beautiful system of the sun, planets and comets could only proceed from the counsel and dominion of an intelligent and powerful Being.'

rows.prompt: Name and explain one traditional image of God.
rows.model_answer: God as father: Jesus called God his father, using the intimate word 'Abba', and taught his followers to pray 'Father, hallowed be your name' (Luke 11:1-4). This image shows God caring for humanity as a parent cares for a child, protecting and guiding them. It is only one part of God's identity, which can never be fully known in this life.

rows.prompt: Explain the image of God as mother and give two examples from scripture.
rows.model_answer: This image shows God's tender, motherly care and closeness to people. It is a rediscovered image found in scripture. In Isaiah 49:14-15 God is like a woman who cannot forget the child she has borne, and in Matthew 23:37 Jesus compares himself to a mother hen gathering her brood under her wings. Hosea 11:3-4 shows God as a mother teaching her child to walk.

rows.prompt: Why might the image of God as liberator be especially meaningful to some people?
rows.model_answer: God as liberator comes from the call of Moses to free the Israelites from slavery (Exodus 3:7-10). It is empowering for people who are oppressed, because it shows God takes pity on the suffering and supports their struggle for justice. For example, Black Americans during and after slavery sang 'Go Down, Moses' - 'Let my people go'.

rows.prompt: Explain what is meant by the prophetic interpretation of human experience.
rows.model_answer: The prophetic interpretation examines and critiques society in the light of religious belief. Rooted in prayer, prophets challenge the status quo and call for change in behaviour, attitudes and lifestyle so there is greater justice. It goes back to Old Testament prophets like Amos, Jeremiah and Isaiah, and to John the Baptist and Jesus.

rows.prompt: How is Fr Peter McVerry an example of a modern prophet?
rows.model_answer: Since 1974 Fr McVerry, a Jesuit, has worked with disadvantaged young people and homeless people in Dublin. He challenges a society that tolerates division and inequality, calling for a truly Christian response to poverty. He set up the Peter McVerry Trust, a national homeless charity, and in his book The Meaning is in the Shadows he shows that those in the shadows are 'God's favourites'.

rows.prompt: How is the mystical interpretation different from the prophetic interpretation?
rows.model_answer: The prophetic interpretation starts with challenging society and calling for justice. The mystical interpretation instead begins with an inner journey, leaving behind the world's distractions to know God personally through meditation, prayer and contemplation. It uses imagination rather than logic, though the greatest mystics, like Henri Nouwen, also speak of compassion and care for others.

rows.prompt: Give two examples of the holy interpretation of life in Christianity or Judaism.
rows.model_answer: In Christianity, Baptism celebrates a new member of the community, with water as a sign of new life and white robes showing new life in Christ. In Judaism, Shabbat is the holiest day: from sundown Friday to sundown Saturday Jewish people rest from all work and spend the day in study and prayer. These moments show life's events as sacred, with God present.

rows.prompt: Summarise St Anselm's argument for the existence of God.
rows.model_answer: Anselm said that 'God' means the greatest being that can be conceived. Existing in reality is greater than existing only in the mind. So if God existed only in the mind, he would not be the greatest conceivable being; therefore God must exist in reality. Since Kant this has been called the ontological argument.

rows.prompt: Compare the understanding of God found in one traditional image of God with the understanding of God found in one contemporary image of God.
rows.model_answer:
A traditional image of God is God as creator. In Genesis, God creates the world and humanity and sees that it is good: 'So God created humankind in his image ... male and female he created them' (Gn 1:27). This image links God to the beauty and diversity of nature and expresses the belief that God existed before creation. It is shown in Michelangelo's Creation of Adam in the Sistine Chapel, where a powerful, fatherly God reaches out to give life. Like other traditional images, it tends to stress God's power and often presents God as male.

A contemporary image is God as mother. Many say this image is not new but rediscovered from scripture. In Isaiah 42:14 God is like a woman in labour; in Isaiah 49:14-15 a woman who cannot forget her child; and in Matthew 23:37 Jesus speaks of gathering Jerusalem's children 'as a hen gathers her brood under her wings'.

Similarity: both show God as the source of life who cares for creation. Difference: the creator image stresses God's power and distance, existing before all things, while the mother image stresses God's tenderness, intimacy and nurturing care. The mother image also reminds us that 'God is neither man nor woman' and that male images reflect the patriarchal societies where they began.

May refer to: father (Abba, Luke 11), creator (Gn 1:27, Creation of Adam), all-powerful protector (omnipotent, slavery); mother (Is 42:14, 49:14-15, Mt 23:37, Hos 11), liberator (Ex 3, Go Down Moses), love (prodigal son); power vs care; maleness and patriarchy; 'God is neither man nor woman'.

rows.prompt: Using examples, explain how a relationship with God can be expressed through the prophetic and the aesthetic ways of interpreting human experience.
rows.model_answer:
The prophetic interpretation critiques society in the light of religious belief. Rooted in prayer, the prophet challenges the status quo and calls for justice, following Amos, Jeremiah, Isaiah, John the Baptist and Jesus. Fr Peter McVerry SJ is an example. In 1974 he went to live in Dublin's inner city and worked with young people affected by poverty, drugs and crime. Shocked by what he saw, he has spent his life challenging a society that tolerates inequality and set up the Peter McVerry Trust for homeless people. In The Meaning is in the Shadows he says those in the shadows are 'God's favourites' and that 'God became one of them'. His relationship with God is expressed through action for justice.

The aesthetic interpretation expresses faith through art, music and poetry, because great beauty suggests the presence of God. Marc Chagall's White Crucifixion shows Jesus the Jew, wrapped in a tallit, crucified between communist soldiers and Nazis desecrating a synagogue, representing the suffering of all Jewish people. It is a favourite of Pope Francis, showing how art from one faith can speak to another. John Shea's poem calls God 'the poetry of wordless lives' and 'the tightening hope that someone has stretched a net beneath this high wire act of ours', expressing a relationship with a God who gives meaning and protection.

rows.prompt: Imagine that Anselm and Aquinas are taking part in a discussion about the existence of God with people today. Outline the ideas that each could put forward to prove the existence of God.
rows.model_answer:
St Anselm (1033-1109), Archbishop of Canterbury and 'father of scholasticism', would begin from faith but argue that God's existence is also reasonable. He would say that the word 'God' means the greatest being that can be conceived. Existing in reality is greater than existing only in the mind. So if God existed only in our minds, we could imagine something greater - a God who really exists. Therefore God must exist in reality. Since Kant this has been called the ontological argument. It may seem strange today, but it has a definite logic.

St Thomas Aquinas (1225-1274) lived when reason was admired and wanted to make faith reasonable. He would offer five proofs. First, the prime mover: nothing moves itself, so there must be a first mover, God. Second, the cause of existence: nothing creates itself, so there must be an uncreated creator, the first cause. Third, there must be a necessary being on which all others depend. Fourth, degrees of perfection: we judge qualities like goodness against a perfect standard, which is God. Fifth, supreme intelligence: the universe is ordered towards regular ends, so it must be directed by an intellect, God.

Both would say these are not scientific proof or blind faith but signposts showing that belief in God is reasonable.

rows.prompt: Explain and give an example of the mystical interpretation of human experience.
rows.model_answer:
The mystical interpretation seeks to make an inner journey, leaving behind the distractions of the world, in order to know God in a personal and intense way. Unlike the prophetic interpretation, its starting point is not challenging society. It uses imagination rather than logic, and through meditation, prayer and contemplation a person may experience God. It is found in all faiths and has become popular today, perhaps because of the fast pace of life and growing materialism.

An example is St Therese of Lisieux. Born in France in 1873, she experienced a mystical union with Christ while preparing for her First Holy Communion and entered the Carmelite Monastery of Lisieux in 1888. She grew close to God through prayer and contemplation and died at only twenty-four, becoming known through her writings as 'The Little Flower'. Her saying, 'What matters in life is not great deeds, but great love', shows that mystics also care about love for others. She was canonised in 1925 and named a Doctor of the Church in 1997.
